Step-by-Step Audio Guided Tour: Salem witch trials walking tour, Salem, MA
Tour-Category: walking

Stop 1: Salem Witch Trials Memorial

Address: Liberty Street, Salem, MA 01970

Coordinates: 42.5201, -70.8951

Type/Specialty: Historical Memorial

Specific Examples: Memorial stones for the victims, inscriptions of their names, a peaceful garden setting.

Orientation: You are about to embark on a walking journey through Salem, MA. This route takes you from the Salem Witch Trials Memorial to the Salem Witch Museum, covering approximately 813 meters through a city steeped in history, where colonial architecture and cobblestone streets echo the past. Your first stop is Salem Witch Trials Memorial. Turn left onto Hawthorne Blvd and continue until you reach Liberty St. The memorial will be on your right. You might notice the historical architecture of the surrounding buildings as you walk. Step through the low stone entryway and pause a few strides in, where the granite benches jut from the grassy earth like unfinished sentences.

The Salem Witch Trials Memorial stands just off Charter Street, on Liberty Street, as Salem's tribute to the twenty women and men executed in 1692. The memorial’s form is quiet but insistent: twenty granite benches, each bearing a name, a date, and the final words of those condemned. On June 10, 1692, neighbors claimed Bridget Bishop’s specter tormented them, and poppets—small figures—were found in her cellar. Bishop’s bench marks not only her name and date of death, but also the echoes of testimony that turned daily life in Salem into a crucible of suspicion, where everyday objects became tools of accusation. Another bench honors Sarah Good, who was hanged on July 19, 1692. The words inscribed on the stone reflect the defiance and emotion of the accused, persisting beyond the moment of their deaths and threading through Salem’s collective memory. Each bench here is a record of community rupture—neighbors accusing neighbors, ordinary routines upended by fear and hysteria. The memorial, dedicated in 1992, was Salem’s first public monument to these events.

Directions: From the Salem Witch Trials Memorial, stroll down Liberty Street, taking in the historical vibe of the area. As you walk, you'll pass the beautiful gardens of the Old Burying Point Cemetery on your left. Continue straight until you reach the intersection with Turner Street, where you’ll see the iconic House of the Seven Gables ahead, just a short walk away. Continue to The House of the Seven Gables.

Stop 2: The House of the Seven Gables

Address: 115 Derby St, Salem, MA 01970

Coordinates: 42.5167, -70.8954

Type/Specialty: Historic House Museum

Specific Examples: The iconic gabled roof, period furnishings, and guided tours of the historic home.

Orientation: Stand before the slate-gray façade, where the seven gables shoulder the weight of three centuries. The wind from Salem Harbor carries the tang of salt and the creak of old timbers. From here, the angles of the house rise against the sky — a vantage once familiar to merchant John Turner and, later, to those who shaped a legend from these eaves.

In 1668, John Turner, a sea captain and merchant, built this house on the harbor’s edge. Its seven gables gave the home its name, and the Turner family’s fortunes, earned through maritime trade, held it for three generations. A story of accusation and consequence played out not far from here: Mary Warren, one of the accusers in 1692, claimed that Ann Pudeator’s specter knocked John Turner II out of a cherry tree. In this single incident, the boundaries between daily life and the chaos of the trials blurred — the Turners’ own orchard became entangled in a web of fear and retribution. Hawthorne’s tale followed a New England family haunted by the legacy of their ancestral home, drawing on the real house as a setting and on his own ancestors’ entanglements in the trials. The character of Judge Pyncheon, shadowed by guilt and unrepentant for his role in the suffering of others, mirrored Hawthorne’s ancestor Judge John Hathorne, who, unlike other judges and jurors, never apologized for his actions in 1692. The house endures, a vessel for memories and myth, its beams holding stories that cross generations.

Directions: From The House of the Seven Gables, stroll down the charming streets of Salem, taking in the historic homes around you. Head west on Turner Street, then take a left onto Essex Street, where you’ll pass by a mix of quaint shops and cafes. Continue to The Witch House
Address: 310 Essex St, Salem, MA 01970
Coordinates: 42.5193, -70.8959
Type/Specialty: Historic House Museum
Specific Examples: The only remaining structure with direct ties to the witch trials, period architecture, and exhibits on witchcraft.
Orientation: As you stand before the sharply gabled silhouette of The Witch House, the street hum recedes beneath the weight of its dark, weathered boards. This is the home of Judge Jonathan Corwin, its eaves dipping low over the sidewalk—look for the original hand-hewn beams, warped and blackened with centuries of salt air. To your right, the windows’ diamond panes catch the daylight, fractured as if to remind you: history here arrives in shards. Step closer, and the wood beneath your hand is rough, each groove a record of New England’s raw climate and the relentless years since 1675. The story that lingers strongest here is not one of superstition, but of the people tied to this house. In 1675, Jonathan Corwin commissioned Daniel Andrews to finish its construction. In the fevered months of accusation, Daniel Andrews was himself named as a witch. The record holds that Andrews, fearing for his life, fled Salem and left his work behind. The beams above you and the floors beneath your feet are the literal result of Andrews’ hands—yet the accusation shattered his place in the community he helped build. The web of suspicion reached even deeper. Unlike Andrews, Thacher faced no warrant—her wealth and family connections shielded her where others fell. The surviving records note her name among the accused, but they also record her freedom, a stark measure of how status shaped outcomes in those frantic days. Inside, the house holds relics—objects passed down or discovered, never belonging to witches, but to the families who survived and remembered. Each floorboard, uneven and creaking, marks the collision of labor, accusation, and privilege. Just ahead, the Salem Witch Museum will widen the lens to the full sweep of a community in crisis.
Directions: As you continue, you'll pass the charming storefronts and cafes, keeping an eye out for the Old Burying Point Cemetery on your left. Just a little further along, you'll find the Salem Witch Museum on your right, with its distinctive facade inviting you to explore more about the town's fascinating history.

Stop 4: Salem Witch Museum — it is roughly 400 meters away.

Continue to The Witch House.

Stop 4: Salem Witch Museum

Address:

Coordinates: 42.5205, -70.8953

Type/Specialty: Museum

Specific Examples: Life-size dioramas of the trials, historical exhibits, and a gift shop.

Orientation: Stand just outside the deep-red stone building with its Gothic arches and pointed windows—a former church now bearing the Salem Witch Museum’s sign.

The Salem Witch Museum’s presentations use life-size sets and narration to immerse you in the world of colonial Massachusetts. The accusations that began in Salem Village soon spread to neighboring towns, disrupting daily routines of work, churchgoing, and market life. At least five people died in jail—not by verdict, but from disease and neglect—while the town’s sense of normalcy was shattered and neighbors grew suspicious of one another. These stories focus on ordinary lives thrown into crisis.

Roger Conant, the Puritan who founded Salem in 1626, died in 1679, thirteen years before the trials began. He never witnessed the hysteria that would take hold, nor saw how the place he named for “peace” would become known for accusation and spectacle. His absence stands as a ghostly counterpoint to the chaos that followed, reminding us that communities can change in ways their founders never anticipate.

The museum building itself carries layers of history. In the mid-19th century, long after the trials, a mob attacked an immigrant neighborhood on the edge of Salem Common, directly facing the East Church. The violence spilled into the streets, showing that suspicion and exclusion persisted in new forms even after the trials ended.

As you leave the museum’s echoing halls, the sounds of traffic and distant laughter draw you back into present-day Salem—a town still shaped by the stories, rituals, and reckonings that began here centuries ago.

Across these stops, one thread runs through: the history of the seventeenth century. Set side by side, they trace how this place changed across the seventeenth century. That's 5 stops in all.
